title: Resistant starch, microbial butyrate and tight-junction regulation
proposition: Dietary resistant starch may regulate epithelial paracellular tight-junction function through microbial butyrate production and local exposure.
rationale: Selected resistant-starch preparations support microbial butyrate production, and direct butyrate exposure can influence epithelial junction assembly. These separate observations motivate testing the joined dietary pathway; they do not establish it.

contextual.explanation: Supports community- and formulation-dependent upstream fermentation, not a downstream tight-junction mechanism.
Butyrate-exposed epithelial models inform plausibility, not dietary resistant-starch mediation.

evidence_sources.label: Peng et al. (2009)
evidence_sources.proposition: Direct butyrate exposure supports AMPK-related junction assembly in Caco-2 monolayers.
evidence_sources.limitations: Purified exposure and cell model; not resistant-starch-derived epithelial exposure.

evidence_sources.label: Moreau et al. (2004)
evidence_sources.proposition: In RS3-fed colitic rats, increased mucosal butyrate utilisation followed healing.
evidence_sources.limitations: Infused labelled butyrate uptake was not tracing starch carbon. Histological healing and substrate use do not establish paracellular tight-junction mediation.

evidence_sources.label: Acute human colonic biopsy experiment (2020)
evidence_sources.proposition: Acute 5 or 25 mM butyrate pretreatment did not prevent induced hyperpermeability ex vivo.
evidence_sources.limitations: Chemical injury and acute exposure; not a universal refutation of dietary or chronic effects.

evidence_sources.label: Controlled potato/bagel dietary trial (2022)
evidence_sources.proposition: The tested potato diet lowered small-intestinal permeability indices but not the colonic probe; it did not establish butyrate-mediated tight-junction regulation.
evidence_sources.limitations: Metabolic syndrome, short dietary periods and surrogate permeability measures; formulation effects and alternative pathways remain.

evidence_sources.label: Scharf et al. (2025)
evidence_sources.proposition: Direct 100 mmol/L colonic butyrate perfusion for 90 minutes reduced induced transcellular hyperpermeability in IBS biopsies compared with pre-exposure.
evidence_sources.limitations: Transcellular outcome is not demonstrated paracellular tight-junction regulation. Direct perfusion is not dietary delivery and does not establish the resistant-starch pathway.

limitations: No joined dietary resistant-starch → butyrate → paracellular tight-junction mechanism has been established by the evidence reviewed here. This is a bounded assessment, not a claim that no such study exists anywhere.
Starch preparation, microbial degraders/cross-feeding, regional exposure and host state affect the pathway.
Faecal butyrate is not production flux or epithelial exposure; transcripts, electrical resistance, histology and paracellular marker flux are distinct endpoints.
Do not collapse human transcellular protection or small-intestinal permeability improvement into a colonic paracellular tight-junction result.
alternative_explanations: Other fermentation products, microbial shifts, altered bile acids, immune effects or nonfermentation food components may mediate a barrier result.
Mucosal healing may increase butyrate uptake rather than be caused by it.
required_evidence: A defined dietary preparation linked to local butyrate exposure and appropriate paracellular/junction endpoints, with credible causal mediation and microbial/host context addressed.
Starch-carbon tracing is one useful approach, not a mandatory exclusive admission criterion; perturbation, rescue and convergent mediation evidence may also be informative.
Separate paracellular from transcellular effects and measured exposure from inferred metabolite availability.
